title: Hemophilia
covers: Hemophilia A and B: inheritance, severity, joint and life-threatening bleeds, diagnosis, prophylaxis and factor dosing, treatment by bleed site, inhibitors and bypassing agents, emicizumab, novel therapies, and acquired hemophilia.

ul: X-linked recessive bleeding disorder: absent or low factor VIII (hemophilia A) or factor IX (hemophilia B)
Lifelong joint, muscle and deep tissue bleeding
The second most common bleeding disorder after VWD; hemophilia A is ~80% of patients
Congenital: F8/F9 mutations on the X chromosome; males are affected in > 99% of cases. Inherited in 2/3; about 1/3 of patients have a new mutation (no family history).
Severe hemophilia A: inversion in intron 22 of F8. Hemophilia B: about 2/3 have missense mutations.
Acquired: a rare autoimmune disorder with autoantibodies against factor VIII

items.p: Case: a 2½-year-old boy with a growing forehead hematoma without trauma, easy bruising, a painful swollen knee at 18 months and a bleeding maternal uncle. Hb 9.5 g/dL, normal platelets and PT, prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing. Factor VIII 0.5% = severe hemophilia A.

items.note: Slide 4 places both F8 and F9 at Xq28. Standard sources: F8 is at Xq28, F9 at Xq27. Not tested.

items.p: Baseline factor levels generally match bleeding severity.

table: Spontaneous joint and muscle bleeds without trauma
Occasional spontaneous bleeds; prolonged bleeding after minor trauma or surgery
Spontaneous bleeding rare; severe bleeding with major trauma or surgery

items.p: Hemarthrosis is the most common bleed (70–80% of all bleeds).

ul: Early signs: worsening pain, tingling or a bubbling feeling, less range of motion
Later: limited movement, swelling, numbness, warm skin
Target joint: bleeding into the same joint ≥ 3 times in 6 months → progressive damage, crippling arthropathy, muscle atrophy

items.caption: Repeated hemarthrosis leads to hemophilic arthropathy

items.p: Blood in the joint → inflammation → synovitis and more bleeding → cartilage loss and joint-space narrowing → contractures, muscle atrophy and chronic pain. Damage is permanent and often needs surgery; its extent tracks the frequency of bleeding.

items.note: Slide 8 gives joint sites as ankle 42%, elbow 21%, knee 20%, shoulder 4%, hip 4%, wrist 2%. Many standard sources name the knee as the most commonly affected joint overall (the ankle leads in young children). The ranking is not tested.

table: Muscle and nerve damage if untreated

ul: Clues: bleeding after circumcision or umbilical cord separation; joint, muscle or deep tissue bleeds; positive family history; ecchymoses, hemarthrosis, arthropathy, muscle atrophy
Labs: prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing; FVIII or FIX < 40%; normal VWF antigen and activity; mutated F8/F9
A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia
If in doubt: factor VIII level → if normal, factor IX → if both normal, factor XI

items.p: WFH 2020: prophylaxis is the standard of care everywhere, and it beats on-demand therapy (treating bleeds when they happen).

ul: Regular, long-term prophylaxis keeps joints and muscles working, prevents chronic arthropathy and gives a good quality of life
Start early: ideally before age 3 or after the first joint bleed (primary prophylaxis)
Aim for trough levels high enough to prevent all bleeds (often ≥ 3–5%)
Dose by the patient's pharmacokinetics

items.p: Case continued: standard half-life factor VIII 3 times a week plus extra doses for bleeds, a central venous catheter, and family teaching on adherence.

ul: Treat at home within 2 hours of onset, supervised by the comprehensive care team
Medicines: factor replacement, cryoprecipitate (FVIII, fibrinogen, factor XIII, VWF, fibronectin), desmopressin, antifibrinolytics
WFH prefers factor concentrates to cryoprecipitate or FFP (quality, safety, efficacy); those are for when nothing else is available or affordable
Treat veins with care

items.p: Example: a 20-kg boy needing a 40 IU/dL rise of factor VIII needs 40 ÷ 2 × 20 = 400 units; factor IX needs twice that per kg.

table: Urgent factor replacement before any evaluation, until bleed-free
Factor until bleed-free + RICE + analgesia + physiotherapy
Antifibrinolytics and supportive care; factor for severe refractory bleeds

items.p: Continuous factor infusion is recommended around surgery or for a severe bleed.

items.note: Slide 16 also lists treatment durations and target peak levels (e.g. intracranial 10–14 days, 50–80/80–100%). These differ from the WFH 2020 tables cited on the slide, so they are not tested.

ul: RICE, physiotherapy, noncontact sports
No NSAIDs or aspirin; control pain
Psychosocial support, vaccinations, patient and family education
Monitor: bleeds, musculoskeletal status, inhibitor development, transfusion-related infections, quality of life

items.p: Prerequisites for care: a multidisciplinary team (hematologists, orthopedic surgeons, physiotherapists, genetic counselors, nurses, psychologists, social workers), management protocols, a coagulation lab able to test for inhibitors, concentrates and antifibrinolytics, and a registry of treatment and bleeding records.
Case continued: at 12 years, the adherent boy has profuse rectal bleeding (Hb 5.0 g/dL) that continues despite factor VIII given to 80–100%. Cause: an inhibitor.

ul: Neutralizing antibodies bind FVIII/FIX and stop it binding to platelet surfaces and other clotting factors
Frequency in severe disease: ~25% in hemophilia A, ~5% in hemophilia B
Titer in Bethesda units: low < 5 BU, high > 5 BU
Consequences: uncontrollable bleeding, progressive joint damage, poor quality of life, very high cost, premature death (hemophilia A-related death 41.7% with inhibitors vs 12.0% without)
Very high doses of factor for a long time
Bypassing agents: activated prothrombin complex; recombinant factor VIIa
Factor VIII mimetic: emicizumab

items.p: rFVIIa binds tissue factor and makes a little thrombin; at high (pharmacological) doses it activates factor X directly on activated platelets, bypassing VIII and IX → thrombin burst → stable plug.

items.caption: Emicizumab bridges factor IXa and factor X

items.p: Emicizumab: a subcutaneous bispecific monoclonal antibody that mimics FVIIIa. It binds FIXa and FX so that FIXa activates FX.

items.note: Slide 20 says activated prothrombin complexes contain activated II, VII, IX and X. Standard sources describe them as mostly non-activated II, IX and X with activated VII. Not tested.

items.p: Limits of standard half-life factor VIII:

ul: IV route: needs venous access, a heavy treatment burden, poor adherence
Rapid elimination: repeated infusions each week, a fluctuating effect
Immunogenicity: alloantibodies → treatment failure, need to bypass FVIII and remove the antibodies

items.p: Extended half-life concentrates mean fewer doses: rFIX half-life 4–5 times longer, rFVIII 1.4–1.5 times longer. Gene therapy offers a potential cure (lasting production of the patient's own FVIII or FIX).
Shared decision-making: seek participation → help explore and compare options → assess preferences → reach a joint decision → evaluate the decision.

Case 2: a 65-year-old woman with 12 hours of abdominal distension, 2 weeks of bruising and hip pain, and 5 years of joint pains and rash. No family history. Hb 5.5 g/dL, normal PT, markedly prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing, FVIII < 1%, very high inhibitor titer; ultrasound shows a massive abdominal hematoma.

ul: A rare, potentially life-threatening autoimmune disorder: autoantibodies against clotting factors, most often FVIII
A disease of older people: > 80% of cases are ≥ 65 years
An underlying condition in 50%: pregnancy, autoimmune disorders, malignancy, drug allergy
Treatment: as for congenital hemophilia with inhibitors, plus treating the underlying disease

Avoid NSAIDs and aspirin

questions.stem: A 2½-year-old boy has a forehead hematoma that has grown for a day without trauma. He bruises easily and had a painful swollen knee at 18 months. His maternal uncle has a bleeding disorder. Platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: A male toddler with deep and joint bleeding, a maternal uncle affected, and an isolated prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing: hemophilia. A: Mucocutaneous; usually not hemarthrosis. B: Normal platelet count. D: Prolongs the PT. E: Would not correct on mixing.

questions.stem: A boy with recurrent hemarthroses has a factor VIII level of 0.5%. How is his disease classified?
questions.explanation: FVIII 0.5% = severe hemophilia A (< 1%). A: 1–< 5%. B: 5–< 40%. C: Factor IX, not VIII. D: Factor IX, not VIII.

questions.stem: A boy has hemophilia, an X-linked recessive disorder; his maternal uncle is also affected. His mother has never bled. What is her most likely status?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is X-linked recessive; with an affected maternal uncle the mother most likely carries the mutated F8/F9 gene and passes it to her son. B: She has never bled. C: The uncle points to her side. D: Less likely with an affected uncle. E: She has never bled.

questions.stem: In what share of cases does hemophilia affect males?
questions.explanation: X-linked recessive in 2/3 of cases; F8/F9 mutations on the X chromosome affect males in > 99% of cases. A: Too low. C: Too low. D: The share that is inherited. E: Too low.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is the second most common bleeding disorder after which disorder?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia is the 2nd most common bleeding disorder after VWD. A: A rare bleeding disorder. B: A rare bleeding disorder. C: A rare platelet disorder. E: A rare bleeding disorder.

questions.stem: About what share of people with hemophilia have hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Hemophilia A makes up ~80% of the total hemophilia population. B: Too low. C: The share with hemophilia B. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia A has no family history of bleeding. Both parents are well. What best explains this?
questions.explanation: About 1/3 of patients have novel mutations; inheritance explains the other 2/3. A: Hemophilia is X-linked. B: A father gives his son a Y. C: Rare; a disease of old age. E: Not the usual explanation.

questions.stem: Which F8 gene defect is associated with severe hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia A is associated with an inversion in intron 22 of the F8 gene. A: Not described. C: Hemophilia B. D: von Willebrand disease. E: Not described.

questions.stem: Which mutation type is found in about two thirds of patients with hemophilia B?
questions.explanation: Around 2/3 of patients with hemophilia B have missense mutations. A: Severe hemophilia A. B: Not the majority. D: Not the majority. E: Not described.

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia A has a factor VIII level of 15%. Which bleeding pattern is expected?

options.E: Bleeding with major surgery or trauma

questions.explanation: Mild (5–< 40%): spontaneous bleeding rare; severe bleeding with major trauma or surgery. Baseline FVIII/IX levels generally correlate with bleeding severity. A: Severe (< 1%). B: Moderate (1–< 5%). C: Moderate (1–< 5%). D: Not the mild pattern.

questions.stem: A boy has spontaneous knee and ankle bleeds without trauma. Which factor VIII level is most likely?
questions.explanation: Severe hemophilia (< 1%): spontaneous joint/muscle bleeding in the absence of trauma. B: Occasional spontaneous bleeding. C: Spontaneous bleeding rare. D: Normal or near normal. E: Normal.

questions.stem: Which severity group makes up the largest share of patients with hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Severe 53%, mild 28%, moderate 19% of patients. A: 28%. B: 19%. C: Not a severity group. E: Rare.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia feels tingling and a bubbling sensation in his knee. The knee is not yet swollen. What is happening?
questions.explanation: Early signs: worsening pain, tingling or bubbling, decreased range of motion. Later: limited movement, swelling, numbness, warm skin. A: Late, after repeated bleeds. B: Fever, swelling, warmth. D: Not in the joint. E: Not the picture.

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia has bled into his right ankle four times in five months. What is this joint called?
questions.explanation: Target joint: bleeding in the same joint ≥ 3 times over a 6-month period, leading to progressive joint damage, crippling arthropathy and muscle atrophy. A: Not the term. C: Not the term. D: The end result, not the definition. E: A late consequence.

questions.stem: What share of all bleeds in hemophilia are joint bleeds?
questions.explanation: Hemarthrosis is the most common type of bleeding, 70–80% of all bleeds. A: Muscle bleeds. B: Neck/throat and GI. C: Intracranial. D: Too low.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old with severe hemophilia has a narrowed knee joint space and a contracture after years of bleeds into that knee. Which process links the bleeds to the damage?
questions.explanation: Blood in the joint → inflammation → synovitis and recurring hemarthrosis → loss of cartilage, narrowing of joint space → contractures, muscle atrophy, chronic pain; permanent arthropathy often requiring surgery. A: Gout. B: Not the cycle. D: Rheumatoid arthritis. E: Not the cycle.

questions.stem: What does the extent of hemophilic joint disease correlate with?

options.A: The half-life of the factor used

questions.explanation: The extent of joint disease correlates with the frequency of bleeding. A: Not the stated correlation. B: Not the stated correlation. C: Not the stated correlation. D: Normal in hemophilia.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia develops a neck swelling and stridor after a throat infection. What is the main danger?
questions.explanation: Neck/throat bleeding is a life-threatening medical emergency leading to airway obstruction. A: Intracranial bleeding. B: Joint bleeding. C: Deep muscle bleeding. E: Gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old with severe hemophilia has an iliopsoas bleed. If untreated, what is the main risk?
questions.explanation: Muscles, especially deep compartments (iliopsoas, calf, forearm), 10–20% of bleeds: can result in muscle and nerve damage if left untreated. B: Neck/throat bleeding. C: Joint bleeding. D: Intracranial bleeding. E: Gastrointestinal bleeding.

questions.stem: Which bleed in hemophilia is classified as life-threatening?
questions.explanation: Life-threatening: intracranial, neck/throat, gastrointestinal. Serious/debilitating: joints, muscles, mucous membranes. A: Serious/debilitating. C: Serious/debilitating. D: Mucous membranes; serious. E: Serious/debilitating.

questions.stem: A male newborn bleeds heavily after circumcision. Platelets and PT are normal; the aPTT is prolonged and corrects on mixing. Which level is measured first?
questions.explanation: If in doubt, do the FVIII level; if normal, the FIX level; if both normal, FXI. A: Second, if VIII is normal. B: Third, if VIII and IX are normal. D: Normal aPTT in XIII deficiency. E: Would prolong the PT.

questions.stem: A boy with suspected hemophilia has a prolonged aPTT that corrects on mixing and a normal factor VIII level. Which test comes next?
questions.explanation: FVIII level first; if normal, FIX level; if both normal, FXI. B: After IX. C: Not in the sequence. D: The PT is normal. E: Not the next step.

questions.stem: A boy with prolonged bleeding has normal factor VIII and factor IX levels and a prolonged aPTT. Which level is measured next?
questions.explanation: If FVIII is normal, do FIX; if both are normal, do FXI. A: Extrinsic; PT. C: Normal aPTT. D: Would prolong the PT. E: Would prolong the PT.

questions.stem: A boy whose maternal uncle has mild hemophilia A bleeds heavily after a tooth extraction. His aPTT is normal. What is the next step?
questions.explanation: A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia; if in doubt, do the FVIII level. A: A normal aPTT does not exclude mild hemophilia. B: Not suggested. C: Not the question here. E: Not the question here.

questions.stem: Which laboratory result is expected in hemophilia A?
questions.explanation: Labs: prolonged aPTT corrected by mixing studies; decreased FVIII or FIX (< 40%); normal VWF Ag/VWF activity; mutated F8/F9 gene. A: Normal in hemophilia. B: Normal in hemophilia. C: Corrects (a deficiency). D: Below 40% in hemophilia.

questions.stem: Hemophilia is defined by a factor VIII or IX level below what value?
questions.explanation: Decreased FVIII or FIX (< 40%); mild hemophilia is 5–< 40%. A: Too high. C: Too low. D: Too high. E: Too low.

questions.stem: The parents of a 2-year-old with severe hemophilia A ask whether to give factor only when he bleeds. What does the WFH recommend?
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis is the standard of care: regular, long-term prophylaxis preserves musculoskeletal function, prevents chronic arthropathy and ensures good quality of life. Prophylaxis is superior to on-demand therapy. B: Treating bleeds when they occur; inferior. C: Should start early. D: Concentrates preferred. E: Not for severe hemophilia.

questions.stem: Primary prophylaxis in severe hemophilia should ideally start before what age?
questions.explanation: Prophylaxis should start early, ideally before the age of 3 or after the first joint bleed (primary prophylaxis). A: Not the stated age. B: Too late. D: Too late. E: Too late.

questions.stem: Which trough factor level does WFH prophylaxis usually aim for?
questions.explanation: Aim for target factor trough levels high enough to prevent all bleeds (often ≥ 3–5%), with pharmacokinetic-guided dosing. A: The upper limit of mild hemophilia. B: Too high for a trough. C: Higher than the usual aim. D: Severe range.

questions.stem: How should prophylaxis doses be individualized?
questions.explanation: PK-guided dosing: individualize dosing to the patient's pharmacokinetics. A: Normal in hemophilia. B: Not used. C: Normal in hemophilia. E: Not used.

questions.stem: A toddler with severe hemophilia A starts standard half-life factor VIII three times a week, and a central venous catheter is inserted. Why is the catheter needed?
questions.explanation: Standard half-life FVIII is given IV and eliminated quickly, so repeated infusions are needed each week: venous access, treatment burden, adherence. B: It is IV; emicizumab is subcutaneous. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason. E: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A boy with hemophilia feels an ankle bleed starting at home in the evening. What does WFH advise?

options.B: Infuse factor at home within 2 hours
options.C: Go to the clinic the next morning
options.E: Take ibuprofen and rest the ankle

questions.explanation: Treat bleeds at home within 2 hours of onset under supervision of the comprehensive care team. A: Treat at onset. C: Too late. D: Factor is needed. E: NSAIDs are avoided.

questions.stem: Cryoprecipitate contains each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Cryoprecipitate contains FVIII, fibrinogen, factor XIII, VWF and fibronectin, so it does not treat hemophilia B. A: Present. B: Present. D: Present. E: Present.

questions.stem: Why does WFH prefer clotting factor concentrates to cryoprecipitate or plasma?
questions.explanation: WFH: concentrates are preferred over cryoprecipitate/FFP because of concerns about quality, safety and efficacy; those are used only if they are the only available or affordable options. A: Cryoprecipitate/FFP are used when affordable. B: Not the reason. C: Still IV. D: Inhibitors arise to concentrates.

questions.stem: A 20-kg boy with severe hemophilia A needs his factor VIII level raised by 40 IU/dL. About how many units of factor VIII are needed?
questions.explanation: 1 FVIII unit/kg raises plasma FVIII by ~2 IU/dL: 40 ÷ 2 = 20 units/kg × 20 kg = 400 units. A: Uses 1 IU/dL per unit/kg. B: Uses 4 IU/dL per unit/kg. C: Too many. E: Too few.

questions.stem: A 30-kg boy with hemophilia B needs his factor IX level raised by 40 IU/dL. About how many units of factor IX are needed?
questions.explanation: 1 FIX unit/kg raises plasma FIX by ~1 IU/dL: 40 units/kg × 30 kg = 1,200 units. B: Uses 2 IU/dL per unit/kg (factor VIII). C: Too many. D: Too few. E: Too few.

questions.stem: Why is factor VIII infused more often than factor IX?

options.A: It raises levels less per unit
options.B: It needs vitamin K to work
options.C: It is cleared by the kidney

questions.explanation: Half-life of factor VIII 8–12 hours; of factor IX 18–24 hours. A: It raises them more (2 vs 1 IU/dL). B: Neither needs it after infusion. C: Not the reason. D: Not the reason.

questions.stem: A boy receives an IV dose of factor VIII for a bleed. When should a blood sample be drawn to check the peak level?
questions.explanation: Peak clotting factor level: 15–30 minutes after infusion. A: Too late. C: The half-life of FVIII. D: The half-life of FIX. E: Too early.

questions.stem: A teenager with hemophilia has knee pain after a joint bleed. Which analgesic should be avoided?
questions.explanation: Supportive therapy: RICE, physiotherapy, noncontact sports, no NSAIDs or aspirin, pain control, psychosocial support, vaccinations, education. A: Safe for pain. B: Not an antiplatelet drug. D: Not an antiplatelet drug. E: Not an antiplatelet drug.

questions.stem: Which sport best suits a boy with severe hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Supportive therapy includes physiotherapy and noncontact sports. A: Contact sport. B: Contact sport. C: Contact sport. E: Contact sport.

questions.stem: People with hemophilia are monitored regularly for each of the following EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Monitor regularly for bleeds, musculoskeletal complications, inhibitor development, transfusion-related infections and quality of life. A: Monitored. B: Monitored. D: Monitored. E: Monitored.

questions.stem: A boy with severe hemophilia A falls and develops a severe headache and vomiting. What is the first step?
questions.explanation: Intracranial bleeding: urgent clotting factor replacement before evaluation and until bleed-free. A: Treatment comes first. B: Life-threatening bleed. C: The platelets are normal. E: Not for severe hemophilia.

questions.stem: A boy's knee hemarthrosis is treated with factor until bleed-free, RICE and analgesia. What else belongs in the plan?
questions.explanation: Joints: urgent clotting factor replacement until bleed-free + RICE + analgesia + physiotherapy. A: Added for neck/throat bleeds. B: Platelets are normal. C: Not deficient. D: Not indicated.

questions.stem: A man with hemophilia has a gastrointestinal bleed. Besides urgent factor replacement, which treatment is added?
questions.explanation: Gastrointestinal: same as intracranial (urgent factor replacement) plus antifibrinolytics. Neck/throat: plus antifibrinolytics/antibiotics. B: Platelets are normal. C: Not deficient. D: Not the added treatment. E: Added for neck/throat bleeds.

questions.explanation: Low-titer < 5 BU; high-titer > 5 BU. A: Not a category used. B: Bethesda measures neutralizing activity. C: Not a factor inhibitor. D: Not a titer category.

options.D: A lab able to test for inhibitors

questions.stem: Which limitation of standard half-life factor VIII causes repeated infusions every week?
questions.explanation: Standard half-life FVIII: IV administration (venous access, burden, poor adherence), rapid elimination (repeated IV infusions, fluctuating effect), immunogenicity (allo-antibodies → treatment failure). A: Causes treatment failure. C: Causes access problems. D: A result, not the cause. E: Not the cause.

questions.stem: In shared decision-making, which step comes right after assessing the patient's preferences?
questions.explanation: Seek participation → help explore and compare options → assess preferences → reach a joint decision → evaluate the decision. A: The first step. B: Before assessing preferences. D: The last step. E: Not a step.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman has 12 hours of abdominal distension, 2 weeks of bruising and hip pain, and 5 years of joint pains and rash. No relative bleeds. Hb is 5.5 g/dL, PT normal; the aPTT is markedly prolonged and does not correct on mixing. Ultrasound shows a massive abdominal hematoma. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: An older adult with new severe bleeding, a negative family history and an aPTT that does not correct on mixing (FVIII < 1%, very high inhibitor titer): acquired hemophilia. A: Mixing would correct. B: Causes clotting, not massive bleeding. C: Prolongs the PT. D: Mixing would correct.

questions.stem: An older woman with acquired hemophilia A and long-standing autoimmune joint disease is bleeding. Besides bypassing agents, what is essential?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia treatment: the same as congenital hemophilia with inhibitors plus treatment of the underlying disease. A: Neutralized by the inhibitor. B: Neutralized. C: Not deficient. E: Platelets are normal.

questions.stem: Two months after delivery, a 30-year-old woman has extensive bruising. Her aPTT is prolonged with a normal PT and does not correct on mixing; factor VIII is very low. What is the most likely cause?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia is due to an underlying condition in 50% of cases: pregnancy, autoimmune disorders, malignancy, drug allergy. A: Prolongs the PT. C: Mixing would correct. D: Mixing would correct. E: Mixing would correct.

questions.stem: Which group most often develops acquired hemophilia?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia is a disease of old age: > 80% of cases are ≥ 65 years. B: Congenital hemophilia presents then. C: Not the typical group. D: Not the typical group. E: Not the typical group.

questions.stem: Against which factor are the autoantibodies of acquired hemophilia most often directed?
questions.explanation: Acquired hemophilia: autoantibodies (inhibitors) against plasma clotting factors, most frequently FVIII. A: Less often. B: Less often. D: Less often. E: Less often.
